'''Marsha Isack Lester''' is an [[Americans|American]] physical chemist and the Edmund J. Kahn Distinguished Professor of Chemistry at the [[University of Pennsylvania]].<ref name=":0" /> Lester uses both theoretical and experimental methods to study the physical chemistry of volatile organic compounds present in the Earth's atmosphere. Her work focuses on the [[hydroxyl radical]] and [[Criegee intermediate]]s.

==Education==
Lester graduated from [[William Allen High School]] in [[Allentown, Pennsylvania]]. In 1976, she received a [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] from [[Douglass Residential College]], an institution for women at [[Rutgers University–New Brunswick]]. In 1981, she earned her [[Doctor of Science|Ph.D.]] from [[Columbia University]] in the laboratory of [[George W. Flynn]]. Her thesis was ''Vibrational Relaxation Dynamics in Bulk Gases and Supersonic Molecular Beams''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.columbia.edu/cu/chemistry/groups/flynn/publications.html|title=The Flynn Group -- Theses and Publications|website=www.columbia.edu|access-date=2018-08-22}}</ref> From 1981 to 1982, she performed postdoctoral work as a [[National Science Foundation]] fellow at [[Bell Labs|Bell Laboratories]].<ref name=":0" />

==Career==
Lester was the chair of the Division of Laser Science of the [[American Physical Society]]. She also worked for [[American Chemical Society]] and was the chair of the [[United States Department of Energy|Department of Energy's]] Council for Chemical and Biochemical Sciences.

She is currently a professor at [[University of Pennsylvania]] in Philadelphia,<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Marsha I. Lester |work=University of Pennsylvania |url=https://www.chem.upenn.edu/profile/marsha-i-lester}}</ref> where she was the first female chair of the department of chemistry from 2005 to 2009.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.energy.upenn.edu/content/marsha-i-lester|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110319063537/http://www.energy.upenn.edu/content/marsha-i-lester|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 19, 2011|title=Marsha I. Lester {{!}} Pennergy|website=www.energy.upenn.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-08-22}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Ahmed|first=Farooq|date=2017-12-19|title=Q&As with Marsha I. Lester|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=115|issue=5|language=en|pages=831–832|doi=10.1073/pnas.1721202115|issn=0027-8424|pmid=29279378|pmc=5798388|doi-access=free}}</ref> She has been awareded the Edmund J. and Louise W. Kahn Award in the Natural Sciences. She is the founder and currently chair of the Penn Forum for Women Faculty, a group formed to support female faculty at the university.<ref name=":1" /> Lester was editor of the ''[[Journal of Chemical Physics]]'' until 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aip.org/press_release/jcp_editor.html|title=Biography|publisher=[[American Institute of Physics]]|access-date=June 15, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130601211706/http://www.aip.org/press_release/jcp_editor.html|archive-date=June 1, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Research===
Lester's research group utilizes theoretical and experimental approaches to study chemical reactions. She focuses on modeling potential energy surfaces between reactive partners, with an emphasis on [[volatile organic compound]]s present in the Earth's atmosphere. She has published extensively on the interactions and reactions of the hydroxyl radical.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/marsha-i-lester-3vslsg/|title=Marsha Lester|website=www.nasonline.org|access-date=2018-08-22}}</ref> Lester's group was the first to obtain an [[infrared spectrum]] of the [[hydrogen trioxide]] radical. Her lab currently works on modeling the stability of this radical and its [[Conformational isomerism|conformers]].<ref name=":0" />

Currently, her group focuses on [[Photochemistry|photo-induced chemistry]] of Criegee intermediates, an intermediate in the [[alkene]] [[ozonolysis]] pathway. This pathway is a primary oxidation pathway for alkenes in the [[troposphere]] and generates atmospheric hydroxyl radicals. Her lab synthesizes Criegee intermediates in order to further study their chemical reactions using [[spectroscopy]].<ref name=":0" />

Her lab also currently focuses on modeling and observing the collisional quenching of excited hydroxyl radicals. Quenching impacts the concentration of hydroxyl radicals in the atmosphere, and is therefore of environmental interest.

Her research group at the University of Pennsylvania was behind the development of [[open shell]] complexes.
